title: Chapter 79 — The Prairie
paragraphs: To scan the lines of his face, or feel the bumps on the head of this Leviathan — this is something no physiognomist or phrenologist, no reader of character from the face or from the skull, has yet undertaken. Such an enterprise would seem about as hopeful as for Lavater to have scrutinized the wrinkles on the Rock of Gibraltar, or for Gall to have climbed a ladder and felt over the Dome of the Pantheon. Still, in that famous work of his, Lavater not only treats of the various faces of men, but also attentively studies the faces of horses, birds, serpents and fish, and dwells in detail on the changes of expression to be seen in them. Nor have Gall and his disciple Spurzheim failed to throw out some hints about the phrenological characteristics of beings other than man. Therefore, though I am poorly qualified to be a pioneer in applying these two semi-sciences to the whale, I will do my best. I try all things; I achieve what I can.

Regarded physiognomically, the Sperm Whale is an anomalous creature. He has no proper nose. And since the nose is the central and most conspicuous of the features, and since it perhaps most modifies and finally controls their combined expression, it would seem that its entire absence, as an external appendage, must very largely affect the whale's countenance. For as in landscape gardening a spire, cupola, monument or tower of some sort is thought almost indispensable to complete the scene, so no face can be physiognomically in keeping without the raised, open-work belfry of the nose. Knock the nose off Phidias's marble Jove, and what a sorry remainder! Nevertheless, Leviathan is of so mighty a magnitude, and all his proportions are so stately, that the same deficiency which would be hideous in the sculptured Jove is no blemish at all in him. No, it is an added grandeur. A nose on the whale would have been impertinent. As you sail round his vast head in your jolly-boat on your physiognomical voyage, your noble conceptions of him are never insulted by the reflection that he has a nose to be pulled — a pestilent notion that so often insists on intruding even when you look at the mightiest royal beadle on his throne.
In certain respects, perhaps the most imposing view of the Sperm Whale's physiognomy is the full front of his head. Seen from this angle, he is sublime.

In thought, a fine human brow is like the East when troubled with the morning. In the repose of the pasture, the curled brow of the bull has a touch of the grand in it. When the elephant pushes heavy cannon up mountain passes, his brow is majestic. Human or animal, the mystical brow is like that great golden seal affixed by the German emperors to their decrees. It signifies — "God: done this day by my hand." But in most creatures, and even in man himself, the brow is very often a mere strip of alpine land lying along the snow line. Few are the foreheads which, like Shakespeare's or Melancthon's, rise so high and come down so low that the eyes themselves seem clear, eternal, tideless mountain lakes; and in the forehead's wrinkles above them you seem to track the antlered thoughts coming down there to drink, as Highland hunters track the deer's prints in the snow. But in the great Sperm Whale, this high and mighty godlike dignity inherent in the brow is so immensely amplified that, gazing on it in that full front view, you feel the Deity and the dread powers more forcibly than in looking at any other object in living nature. For you see no one point precisely; not one distinct feature is revealed; no nose, eyes, ears or mouth; no face — he has none, properly speaking; nothing but that one broad firmament of a forehead, pleated with riddles, dumbly lowering with the doom of boats, and ships, and men. Nor does this wondrous brow diminish in profile, though viewed that way its grandeur does not overpower you so much. In profile you plainly see that horizontal, half-moon-shaped hollow in the middle of the forehead which, in man, is Lavater's mark of genius.

But how? Genius in the Sperm Whale? Has the Sperm Whale ever written a book or made a speech? No, his great genius is declared in his doing nothing in particular to prove it. It is declared, moreover, in his pyramid-like silence. And this reminds me that had the great Sperm Whale been known to the young Orient World, he would have been deified by the childlike thoughts of its magi. They deified the crocodile of the Nile because the crocodile is tongueless; and the Sperm Whale has no tongue, or at least it is so exceedingly small that it cannot be thrust out. If hereafter any highly cultured, poetical nation shall lure back to their birthright the merry May-day gods of old, and enthrone them, living, once more in the now egotistical sky, on the now unhaunted hill, then be sure that, raised to Jove's high seat, the great Sperm Whale shall lord it there.

Champollion deciphered the wrinkled granite hieroglyphics. But there is no Champollion to decipher the Egypt of every man's and every creature's face. Physiognomy, like every other human science, is nothing but a passing fable. So if Sir William Jones, who could read thirty languages, could not read the deeper and subtler meanings in the simplest peasant's face, how can unlettered Ishmael hope to read the awe-inspiring Chaldee of the Sperm Whale's brow? All I do is set that brow before you. Read it if you can.
